blocks.text: Estimation Reference Numbers: The Pocket Card

The three tables every estimation stands on — the full latency ladder, the powers-of-two size ladder, and the availability nines with their downtime math — each with its sources, its 2026 notes, and its confidence marks.
Why this page exists

The previous lesson, Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation, taught you to lift — state assumptions, round, multiply, sanity-check. But every lift is measured against reference weights, and that lesson deliberately carried only six of them. This page is the full set: the pocket card.

Treat it the way pilots treat a checklist card. You don't read it once and throw it away; you keep it reachable and let your eye land on the row you need. When a case-study lesson after this one says "from the latency ladder" or "at five nines," it means these numbers, so the numbers live in exactly one place and can be trusted — and re-checked — in one place.

One term before the tables, because everything below leans on it: an order of magnitude is one step of ×10. A memory read and a disk seek differ by about five orders of magnitude — five ×10 steps, 100 ns against about 10 ms. Orders of magnitude are the currency of estimation: being wrong by 20 percent is noise, being wrong by ×10 is a different design.
Table 1 — The latency ladder, in full

How long the machine takes to do the things designs are made of. These are the classic numbers published by Peter Norvig and taught at Google from Jeff Dean's talks; the human-scale column uses the previous lesson's scale (an L1 cache fetch = 1 second), so the two lessons interlock. for the values as published; the 2026 notes after the table carry their own marks.
Operation, Real time, If an L1 cache fetch = 1 second
L1 cache reference, 0.5 ns, 1 second
Branch mispredict — the CPU guessed the code's path wrong, 5 ns, 10 seconds
L2 cache reference — the CPU's second-fastest shelf, 7 ns, 14 seconds
Mutex lock / unlock — one thread waits its turn, 25 ns, 50 seconds
Main memory reference, 100 ns, about 3 minutes
Compress 1 KB (Zippy, a compression library), about 3,000 ns, about 100 minutes
Send 1 KB over a 1 Gbps network, about 10,000 ns, about 5½ hours
SSD random read (classic, SATA era), about 150,000 ns, about 3½ days
Read 1 MB sequentially from memory, about 250,000 ns, about 6 days
Round trip inside one datacenter, about 500,000 ns, about 12 days
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD, about 1,000,000 ns, about 3 weeks
Disk seek (spinning disk), about 10,000,000 ns, about 8 months
Read 1 MB sequentially from spinning disk, about 20,000,000 ns, about 15 months
Packet: California → Netherlands → back, about 150,000,000 ns, about 9½ years

How to read it. Find the two operations your design is choosing between; the ratio between their rows is the price of the choice. Reading from memory instead of disk isn't "a bit faster" — it's minutes against months, a factor of about 100,000 for the seek the read replaces. And notice the shape: the ladder spans about eight and a half orders of magnitude, but the gaps bunch — the cache and memory rungs crowd within a step or two of each other, while the jumps to disk and to another continent yawn by factors of twenty or thirty. Those wide gaps are where designs live: crossing one is never an accident, it's the decision.
What changed by 2026. The table's gaps have barely moved — but three rows deserve a modern note before you quote them:

SSD random read: the classic 150 µs is a SATA-era figure. A modern NVMe drive answers a random read in the tens of microseconds — call it about 50 µs, about a day on the human scale. Same rung, faster shoes; quote the modern figure for new designs and the classic one when reading older material.
Compression: the classic row used Zippy at about 3 µs per KB. Modern codecs (Zstd) do the same job in roughly about 1 µs. Compression got about 3× cheaper; it was never the bottleneck rung anyway.

The disk rows are now a legacy tier. Spinning disks still seek in about 10 ms — physics of moving parts — but in 2026 they mostly hold archives and backups, not user traffic. The rows stay on the card because old systems (and old interview material) still speak in disk.

Unchanged, and why: main memory still answers in about 100 ns (modern DDR5 measures 50–100 ns) and the transatlantic packet is bounded by the speed of light. One is a mature technology, the other is physics — neither was ever going to move.
Table 2 — The powers-of-two ladder
Estimates die in unit conversions, so this ladder does the two conversions you'll make constantly: bytes to friendly sizes, and counts to friendly counts.
Power, Bytes (approx.), Friendly name, A familiar anchor
2^10, about 1,000, 1 KB, A short email, a config file
2^20, about 1,000,000, 1 MB, About a minute of MP3 audio
2^30, about 1,000,000,000, 1 GB, Roughly 20–30 minutes of HD video
2^40, about 1 trillion, 1 TB, A typical laptop drive
2^50, about 1 quadrillion, 1 PB, A small company's whole archive

Two facts do the daily work. First, each step up is ×1,024, which estimation rounds to ×1,000 — so 1 GB ≈ 1 million KB, and converting is just counting commas: KB → MB → GB → TB, three orders of magnitude per step. Second, the counts ladder is the same shape: a thousand ≈ 10³, a million ≈ 10⁶, a billion ≈ 10⁹, a trillion ≈ 10¹². When a problem says "a billion events a day," your hand should write 10⁹ before your brain finishes the sentence. The anchors are illustrative approximations, not measurements — they exist so a number has a feel before it has a design.

Worth memorizing alongside: a day ≈ 100,000 seconds (from the previous lesson), a million seconds ≈ 11½ days, and a billion seconds ≈ 32 years. Those two conversions quietly power half the sanity checks you'll ever run — "we keep logs for a billion seconds" should hurt a little when you hear it.
Table 3 — The nines: availability and its downtime price

When a design says "we need 99.99 percent availability," it's really making a promise about downtime. This table prices the promise. The math is one line. A year holds 365 × 24 × 3,600 = 31,536,000 seconds, and downtime is the sliver that's left — 100 percent minus the promise. Four nines promises 99.99 percent up, so the downtime fraction is 0.01 percent: 0.0001 × 31,536,000 = 3,154 seconds ≈ 52.6 minutes a year, and the monthly column is that divided by 12, ≈ 4.38 minutes a month. Every figure in the table comes from that one multiplication, so you can redo any of them on a napkin.
Availability, Downtime per year, Downtime per month, Say it as
99 percent ("two nines"), about 3.65 days, about 7.3 hours, A long weekend, every year
99.9 percent ("three nines"), about 8.76 hours, about 43.8 minutes, One bad workday a year
99.95 percent, about 4.38 hours, about 21.9 minutes, About one afternoon a year
99.99 percent ("four nines"), about 52.6 minutes, about 4.38 minutes, Under an hour a year
99.999 percent ("five nines"), about 5.26 minutes, about 26 seconds, Five minutes a year — gone before you've read the alert
99.9999 percent ("six nines"), about 31.5 seconds, about 2.6 seconds, Half a minute a year

How to read it. Each extra nine divides downtime by ten — and multiplies the engineering bill by far more than ten. Going from three nines to four means your system may only be down about 4.4 minutes a month: no maintenance windows, no "restart it and see," deploys that roll back themselves. Five nines is a lifestyle — it's the telephone network's historic standard — and it costs like one. So the interview move is never to recite the table; it's to ask which row the problem actually needs. Most products are honestly fine at three nines; promising five because it sounds impressive is how teams buy themselves a very expensive 26 seconds a month.
Using this card in the interview room
Three moves, one per table:

Quote the rung, not the number. "A disk seek costs us about 10 ms — on the ladder that's the months rung — so this read has to come from memory or SSD" lands harder than any raw figure, because it shows the ratio doing the deciding.
Convert out loud. "A billion events… that's 10⁹, so about 10⁴ a second over a day" — narrating the powers-of-two step is the estimate's proof of work.

Price the promise. When a requirement says "highly available," answer with a row: "at four nines we're budgeting 52 minutes of downtime a year — is that the target, or is three nines' workday acceptable?" You've just turned a vibe into a decision, which is the whole job.
Dos and don'ts
Do:
Round from these tables, not from memory of other numbers. One trusted card beats five half-remembered blog posts.
Name the era when it matters. Quoting the SATA-era SSD figure for a 2026 design is a small, avoidable own-goal — the 2026 notes are on the card for this.
Redo the nines math instead of reciting it. The multiplication is the credibility.
Don't:
Don't quote a rung you can't place. If you can't say what sits above and below a number, you don't know it yet — look it up on the card, out loud, without shame.
Don't promise a nine you haven't priced. Every nine is a budget, in downtime and in engineering hours.
Takeaways
The full latency ladder spans 0.5 ns to 150 ms — about eight and a half orders of magnitude — and its gaps, not its point values, are what designs are built on.

By 2026 the SSD rung improved (tens of microseconds on NVMe) and compression got cheaper (Zstd), while memory about 100 ns and the transatlantic about 150 ms stand still. Quote the modern figure when the design is modern.
The size ladder is one shape repeated: ×1,000 per step, KB → MB → GB → TB → PB, mirrored by the counts ladder thousand → million → billion → trillion.
The nines are priced in downtime: three nines ≈ a workday a year, four ≈ 52 minutes, five ≈ 5 minutes. Each extra nine divides downtime by ten and multiplies the engineering bill by much more.
This card is the reference for the rest of the course: when a later lesson says "from the ladder" or "at four nines," it means these rows.
